Abstract
We study offline-to-online learning in linear contextual bandits with biased offline
regression data: the offline parameter need not match the online one, so history
should not be treated as a single warm start. We model directional transfer with a
shift certificate (Mshift, ρ) and offline ridge estimation, yielding a geometry-aware
confidence region for the online parameter rather than an isotropic radius. We
propose Ellipsoidal-MINUCB, which combines a standard online branch with an
offline-informed pooled branch and uses offline information only when it tightens
uncertainty. With high probability, regret is bounded by the minimum of a standard
SupLinUCB-style fallback and a pooled term that separates statistical width from a
certificate-weighted shift penalty. Under a simple alignment condition, the pooled
term further simplifies to a rate governed by an effective dimension induced by
the offline geometry. We also show that a purely Euclidean (scalar) shift bound,
by itself, does not determine which feature directions are transferable. Beyond
this fixed certificate, we show how to learn a data-driven certificate from data
at finitely many refresh times and establish a high-probability regret bound for
Ellipsoidal-MINUCB with epoch-wise learned certificates. Experiments match
the main prediction: gains are strongest at intermediate horizons when offline
coverage and transferability align, while the method otherwise tracks the safe
online baseline.

Introduction
Many bandit deployments start with historical logs, A/B traffic, or related populations. Exploiting
this data could reduce cold-start exploration, but the offline model is often trained under a different
decision policy, population, or feature distribution than the live system. The resulting misspecification
is not a small nuisance: treating an offline point estimate as if it were the online truth can be arbitrarily
misleading once deployment begins.
We focus on linear contextual bandits, where arms share a feature map in Rd and rewards are linear
in a shared parameter. This shared-parameter structure changes the question: offline usefulness is not
a list of arm-specific biases, but a problem of which directions in feature space remain informative
for online play.
Usefulness is intrinsically directional. Offline-to-online gap is generally anisotropic: a single
Euclidean radius treats all feature directions equally, which can be simultaneously too loose in stable
directions and too aggressive where shift is large. Analyses of biased prior data at the arm level
(e.g., MIN-UCB) and of mismatch through scalar summaries in simpler action models [Cheung and
Lyu, 2024] do not directly lift to a global linear feature map without an explicit geometric interface.

Prior work on leveraging offline design in linear bandits often studies coverage under the idealization
that the offline and online parameters coincide [Vijayan et al., 2025]. We target the mixed regime:
offline samples may be rich in some directions and misleading in others while the user can supply a
matrix-shaped description of which directions are plausible under shift.
We take as side information a shift certificate ∥θ∗−θ†∥Mshift ≤ρ together with a standard offline
ridge estimate and its design matrix. This yields a confidence description for the online target that
separates statistical error (through the offline Gram) from shift (through (Mshift, ρ)) along each
queried feature direction. The algorithmic object is Ellipsoidal-MINUCB, built on the SupLinUCB
shell [Chu et al., 2011]: a standard online confidence branch and a pooled branch that mixes offline
and online Gram information; UCB/LCB scores are merged so that the pooled information is used
only when it is tighter. The end result is a per-round minimum of online and offline-informed
optimism, hence a retained eO(

Our end goal is not a new generic SupLinUCB-style master rule in isolation, but a modeling and
decision interface for directional misspecification: the certificate and offline design specify which
directions are simultaneously well measured and safe to pool, while a standard online confidence
branch remains a round-by-round fallback; Section 4 makes the ensuing min-type regret bound
explicit. Good offline data combine (i) enough effective sample size to shrink offline regression
error, (ii) a coverage shape in which the directions queried online are actually measured, and (iii) a
conservative but valid shift envelope; increasing data alone does not fix a misspecified shift model
when the online-requested directions are expensive under the certificate.
In practice, a valid (Mshift, ρ) may be unavailable a priori; we therefore also develop a data-driven
certificate updated at finitely many epoch boundaries, with statements, routing formulas, and regret
guarantees in Section 5 and Appendices N.1 and N.
Contributions.
• Directional certificate. We use the directional certificate (Mshift, ρ) as a natural geometric
interface for offline quality: it encodes which directions are transferable and yields a
geometry-aware confidence description rather than a scalar trust radius.
• Algorithm Design. We introduce Ellipsoidal-MINUCB: a two-branch optimistic procedure
with an always-safe online branch and an offline-informed pooled branch; min/max aggrega-
tion ensures the pooled branch only acts when it is tighter, while the online branch remains
a round-by-round fallback. Section 3 also records diagnostic quantities for when pooling
helps in practice.
• Data-driven certificates. When a valid (Mshift, ρ) is not available a priori, we construct a
matrix–radius pair at finitely many epoch boundaries from the offline design matrix and the
online ridge state, using the parallel sum of the two regularized Gram matrices so the center
gap and shift map are measured in a shared norm geometry. The min/max layer policy of
Section 3 is unchanged except for re-parameterized pooled radii and routings (Section 5).
• Theory. We prove a high-probability regret guarantee given by the minimum of the standard
SupLinUCB fallback [Chu et al., 2011] and a geometry-dependent pooled term, and we
show how directional usefulness appears through a pooled-width decomposition. Under an
alignment condition between offline precision and shift, the pooled analysis yields a clean
effective-dimension regime. We also give a separation for purely Euclidean (scalar) shift
summaries (Appendix B). For the epoch-wise data-driven construction in Section 5, we
establish a high-probability regret bound over the epoch boundaries at which the certificate
is updated (proofs in Appendix N).
Organization. Sections 2–6 present the model, Ellipsoidal-MINUCB, main results, data-driven
certificates, and experiments; related work and the conclusion follow. The appendix contains proofs
and supplements, including isotropic and diagonal specializations (Appendices B and K), data-
driven certificate details and proofs (Appendices N.1 and N), notation (Appendix C), and additional
experiments (Appendix O).

Experiments
We evaluate Ellipsoidal-MINUCB in synthetic linear contextual bandits with K=5 arms, d=5
features, horizon T=20000, sub-Gaussian reward noise σ=0.1, and noff=2000 offline points. Arms’

Related Work
A broad offline-to-online literature studies how historical data, hints, or source models can reduce the
cost of online learning. Warm-start and transfer approaches combine supervised and bandit feedback
[Zhang et al., 2019], use initial hints [Cutkosky et al., 2022], handle deficient support in logged data
[Tran-The et al., 2021], and transfer across contextual bandit tasks [Cai et al., 2024]. Other work
considers weighted hypothesis transfer [Bilaj et al., 2023], partially observed confounded offline
data [Tennenholtz et al., 2021], offline logs in larger sequential settings [Wagenmaker and Pacchiano,
2023, Kausik et al., 2025], and contextual online–offline interaction in pricing [Zhang et al., 2025, Bu
et al., 2020, 2025]. A related offline contextual bandit and off-policy learning line learns or evaluates
policies from logged feedback under support, variance, or pessimism constraints [Dudík et al., 2011,
Swaminathan and Joachims, 2015, Wang et al., 2024, Gabbianelli et al., 2024]. These works establish
many ways in which past data can help decision-making, but their main object is not the online regret
value of biased offline evidence after deployment.
The closest comparisons come from two directions. In linear bandits with offline data, prior observa-
tions can lower exploration cost through offline Gram matrices and design-based exploration when
the offline and online parameters coincide [Vijayan et al., 2025]. In multi-armed bandits with biased
offline data, MIN-UCB shows that a learner should exploit offline samples only when the mismatch
is controlled, and otherwise fall back toward online learning [Cheung and Lyu, 2024]. These two
lines capture the two ingredients we need: coverage in a linear model and safe use of biased offline
information.
What remains open is how to judge offline quality when both ingredients are present in a linear
contextual bandit. Offline coverage alone is not enough because the offline parameter may drift; a
scalar mismatch bound is not enough because actions share features and shift matters by direction.
Our setting therefore asks which feature directions of the offline sample remain reusable online. The
directional certificate is the interface we use to express this quality and to decide when pooled offline
evidence can safely contract online uncertainty.
At the algorithmic level, our online fallback builds on the optimism-based foundations of contextual
and linear bandits: LinUCB and SupLinUCB [Li et al., 2010, Chu et al., 2011], the OFUL analysis
[Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011], and linear Thompson-style approaches [Agrawal and Goyal, 2013].
We also relate to misspecification-robust bandits, where the online reward model may deviate from
the assumed linear class. Classic and follow-up work includes Ghosh et al. [2017] and Takemura
et al. [2021]; more recent developments include Foster et al. [2020] and Krishnamurthy et al. [2021].
Here the online model remains linear; the difficulty is that the offline parameter may differ from the
9


online one in a structured, direction-dependent way. Our contribution is to encode that mismatch
through a directional certificate and use it inside a hybrid pooled/online optimistic rule.
8
Conclusion
A key insight of this paper is that biased offline data in linear contextual bandits are not useful as
a single warm start. They are useful only along directions that are both well covered offline and
stable under offline-to-online shift. The directional certificate (Mshift, ρ) makes this criterion for
offline quality explicit, and Ellipsoidal-MINUCB turns it into a safe algorithmic rule: exploit pooled
geometry where transfer is credible, and fall back to the classical online branch elsewhere.
The analysis preserves this safety story at the regret level: the high-probability bound is the minimum
of a standard SupLinUCB-type online term and a geometry-dependent pooled term. Poor transfer
therefore cannot erase the explicit eO(
√
dT) fallback. The main limitation is that the certificate
is side information, and the pooled term may depend on the online path. Natural next steps are
data-driven certificates with graceful degradation under approximate transfer, and extensions beyond
linear models.

Abstract: We study offline-to-online learning in linear contextual bandits with biased offline regression data: the offline parameter need not match the online one, so history should not be treated as a single warm start. We model directional transfer with a shift certificate (Mshift, ρ) and offline ridge estimation, yielding a geometry-aware confidence region for the online parameter rather than an isotropic radius. We propose Ellipsoidal-MINUCB, which combines a standard online branch with an offline-informed pooled branch and uses offline information only when it tightens uncertainty. With high probability, regret is bounded by the minimum of a standard SupLinUCB-style fallback and a pooled term that separates statistical width from a certificate-weighted shift penalty. Under a simple alignment condition, the pooled term further simplifies to a rate governed by an effective dimension induced by the offline geometry. We also show that a purely Euclidean (scalar) shift bound, by itself, does not determine which feature directions are transferable. Beyond this fixed certificate, we show how to learn a data-driven certificate from data at finitely many refresh times and establish a high-probability regret bound for Ellipsoidal-MINUCB with epoch-wise learned certificates. Experiments match the main prediction: gains are strongest at intermediate horizons when offline coverage and transferability align, while the method otherwise tracks the safe online baseline.
